title: Spritework on the ZX Spectrum: Rendering
text:
Last week’s article saw us preparing sprite graphics for display on the ZX Spectrum’s display screen. This week we’ll actually do the rendering, and kick off the shooting gallery project properly:
It also turns out that the shooting gallery project doesn’t quite exercise all the things we’d need from a sprite renderer, so the main program this week will be a simple test program that just moves a graphic between, and off, all four corners of the screen.
Designing the Rendering Function
This routine is complex enough that we should plan it out first. We won’t have to take it all the way down to functioning C code like we did with Bresenham’s algorithm, but a proper pseudocode structure will do us some good.
We are given a pointer to our preprocessed sprite data along with the X and Y coordinates at which to draw it. The sprite data started out as a monochrome 16×16 bitmap; after
our preprocessing from last week
it is a data structure with the following properties:
It is now an array of 4 24×16 bitmaps.
The first element of the array is horizontally-aligned with attribute cells, with each subsequent element shifted right two pixels.
Within each 24×16 bitmap, the graphics are arranged in column-major order.
These properties are consequences of the decisions we made last week, and these have some implications for our logic here:
We may decompose our 24×16 bitmap into three horizontally-aligned 8×16 bitmaps. This will let us re-use our routines from last week.
We may only place our sprite at even pixel addresses. In most cases we’ll be better served by thinking of X coordinates as ranging from 0 to 127 instead of 0 to 255.
Since the shifted sprites are in sorted order from left to right, the 24×16 image that we
want
may be found by taking the last two bits of the X coordinate and using them as an index into the array.
With this, then, we’re fully equipped to handle cases where the sprite fits entirely on the screen:
Assuming X is in the 0-119 range, take the last two bits, multiply them by 48, and add them to the source pointer. (Each entry is 3 16-byte columns of graphics, so this advances us appropriately through the array.)
Compute the destination pointer from the Y coordinate and the X coordinate with the offset masked out. With our reimagining of screen coordinates, this will be very similar but not identical to the routine we wrote to
plot individual pixels.
Use our unaligned-vertical-copy logic from last week to place each of the three columns of data on the screen at our computed location.
Now we need to handle cases where we’re partially off the screen. In increasing order of complexity:
The right edge
can be detected at render time. If we find ourselves advancing to screen column 32, just stop the loop early.
The left edge
requires some preprocessing. If we find ourselves asked to render to a negative X coordinate, we need to advance both X and the source pointer a whole number of columns while decreasing the total number of columns drawn. Happily, thanks to the way two’s-complement math works, the offset logic here for picking which shifted image to draw works exactly the same with negative numbers as it does with positive ones.
The bottom edge
needs more work
during
the render; we can detect in advance that we should be rendering fewer than 16 rows in each column, but we will then need to advance the source pointer
between
columns to ensure that we start rendering each column from the right point.
The top edge
is similar, but if we’re off the top edge we need to advance the source and destination pointers
before
the render since we’re removing the top rows.
Putting it all together gets us this pseudocode.
Input: SRC (pointer to 192-byte buffer), X (-7 - 127), Y (-15 - 191)
1. Bounds-check: Quit immediately if the sprite is entirely off the screen.
2. Horizontally align data: OFFSET = X MOD 4, SRC = SRC + 48 * OFFSET, X = INT(X / 4)
3. Start assuming full sprite drawn: COLUMNS = 3, ROWS = 16
4. Correct for being off the left edge: while X < 0...
 4a. X = X + 1, COLUMNS = COLUMNS - 1, SRC = SRC + 16
 4b. Quit immediately if COLUMNS = 0.
5. Correct for being off the top edge: if Y < 0...
 5a. ROWS = ROWS + Y. (Still positive thanks to step 1.)
 5b. SRC = SRC - Y.
 5c. Y = 0.
6. Correct for being off the bottom edge: if y > (192 - 16)...
 6a. ... ROWS = ROWS + (192-16) - Y.
7. STRIDE = 16 - ROWS.
8. Convert final X and Y coordinates to a pointer in DEST.
9. Draw the sprite: for I = 1 to COLUMNS...
 9a. Stash DEST.
 9b. for J = 1 to ROWS...
 9b.1. Copy a byte from SRC to DEST.
 9b.2. Increment SRC.
 9b.3. Alter DEST pointer to be to the next row down.
 9c. Restore DEST and increment it to move to the next column.
 9d. If DEST MOD 32 is now 0, quit immediately (off the right edge)
 9e. Add STRIDE to SRC.
Implementation
Now that we have our pseudocode, we can start turning it into
actual
code. This turns out to be more exciting than it looks, and the excitement starts almost immediately.
First we have to nail down the API and that part is straightforward.
HL
will be our source pointer,
D
will be our Y coordinate, and
E
will be our X coordinate. That part isn’t exciting. The part that
is
exciting is that Y’s is stored in an 8-bit register, its legal range runs from -15 through 191, and that’s means it needs to be a signed value that doesn’t work as a normal 8-bit signed value
or
as an 8-bit unsigned value. Bounds-checking this will be a bit tricky.
Fortunately, it’s a trick we’ve already done before, and under harsher conditions; we can manage this with what is basically a cheaper version of
the Atari 2600’s SkipDraw technique.
The key insight is that by adding 15 to our both our Y coordinate and our target bounds, we will now be making a simple
unsigned integer
check on a range that has zero as its lower bound… which, since we are unsigned, means that we will be checking both edges of the range in a single comparison. Bounds-checking the Y coordinate is thus done like this:
draw_sprite:
 ld a,d
 add 15
 cp 192+15
 ret nc
We don’t do our X check yet; it turns out to fall out more naturally later on. Our next step is to horizontally align the data; extracting the lower two bits of the X coordinate and using that to advance
HL
to the appropriate sprite buffer, then converting the X coordinate from a pixel coordinate into a character/byte coordinate. That works out to the two statements
HL += 48 * (E & 3); E = E >> 2
… and we need that shift to be
signed
for this operation. Fortunately, with a valid range of -7 through 127, we
can
treat the X register in E as if it’s an ordinary signed 8-bit value and use the Z80’s arithmetic shift operations to do that work. We don’t have a multiplier, but we can handle it as a loop with no difficulty:
ld a,e
 and 3
 jr z,.x_aligned
 ld bc,48
1 add hl,bc
 dec a
 jr nz,1B
.x_aligned:
 sra e ; Move E from X coord to char offset
 sra e
There’s only one slightly unusual bit there; since I’m using
BC
as the register to hold the value for the 16-bit addition, I’m using
A
as my loop variable here instead of the more usual
B
.
Handling Going Offscreen: X Dimension
With X now converted into a byte coordinate, trimming on the left side will be easier. This is where another interesting facet comes up: It’s
not actually possible to go completely off the screen to the right.
We’re interpreting X as a signed 8-bit value, with a legal range from -7 through 127, and 127 is the highest you can go. A value just off the right side of the screen, by our math here, will be at pixel
-128,
not 128. As a result, we only have to worry about being off the left edge. The logic here works almost exactly like our pseudocode.
ld a,3 ; Number of columns to render
ld bc,16 ; BC = 16 = column size in src
1 bit 7,e ; X coord negative?
jr z,.x_ok ; Once we're on-screen we're done
add hl,bc ; Otherwise skip a column...
inc e ; ... move a character cell right...
dec a ; ... decrement the column count...
ret z ; ... quit if it's zero...
jr 1B ; ... and check again if it's not.
.x_ok: ld c,a ; Save final column count in C
The only part of this that isn’t a completely blind hand-translation is that we check if the X coordinate is negative by doing a bit-test on the sign bit instead of working out a compare. This is handy, because it lets us keep the accumulator untouched by the checks.
In this part and the one before it, we’re starting to see places where the Z80’s extensions over the 8080 pay off in terms of clarity, size, and speed; we’re using larger and slower instructions but what we are
buying
with it is the ability to keep values in static locations in the register bank, saving us considerably
more
time in no-longer-necessary register moves and restores.
Handling Going Offscreen: Y Dimension
We’ve already bounds-checked cases where the sprite is entirely off the screen. That makes our job here somewhat easier; we know that we’re partially off the top of the screen if the Y coordinate in
D
is negative. We must, however, reckon with the fact that we don’t want the values 128-191 to
count
as negative, and that means that a simple sign-bit test like we did with X won’t suffice. The secret here is to once again shift into an unsigned mode of operations: an
unsigned addition that overflows
is the same as a
signed addition that turns a value from negative to positive.
We can detect both with the carry bit. That makes checking for negative values pretty easy:
ld b,16 ; Default row count in B
 ld a,b ; ... are we off the top?
 add d
 jr nc,.check_bottom ; If not, check bottom
There is a small subtlety here: the carry will be set here on any value between -16 and -1… but -16 is fully offscreen and we should not write anything in that case. That’s fine, though, because we trapped that in our initial bounds check. The
reason we do it this way,
though, is that now
A
holds the value of
ROWS + Y
, which we need to compute as step 5A. We save that back to our row count in
B
and then advance
HL
appropriately. We don’t have any spare register pairs anymore, though, so we have to do the addition with 8-bit math:
ld b,a ; If so, correct height...
 ld a,16 ; ... compute ptr offset...
 sub b
 add l ; ...and apply it to source...
 jr nc,1F
 inc h
1 ld l,a
We also have to correct the Y coordinate, but when we’re off the top, that’s trivial; we just set it to zero.
ld d,0 ; ... and set Y to top of screen
 jr .y_ok
Checking the bottom is a bit simpler because we only need to adjust the row count. Once again we do a subtraction instead of a comparison because we want the value again afterwards; the
amount by which the Y coordinate exceeds
the last value where the whole sprite is on screen is the amount we wish to deduct from the row count, and that lets us turn the correction into a simple addition.
.check_bottom:
 ld a,192-16
 sub d
 jr nc,.y_ok
 add b
 ld b,a
Final Preparations Before the Blit
It turns out that we’ll be able to just leave the column count in
C
for our remaining logic, but we’ll be using
B
enough that the total row count needs to be stored for later use. Similarly, we precompute the “stride” count,
16-ROWS
, and store it for easy access later:
.y_ok: ld a,b
 ld (.row_count),a
 ld a,16
 sub b
 ld (.stride),a
Now it’s time for step 8 in our pseudocode: converting
DE
from separate X and Y coordinates into a proper memory address in the screen bitmap. This code is very similar to the code in our
PLOT
routine from the bitmap work; the main difference is that we’ve already shifted away the sub-byte coordinates in X and we need to use
DE
as both source
and
destination. That means we have to use
B
to store temporary values sometimes instead of the ultimate destination bytes:
ld a,d
 and 7
 ld b,a
 ld a,d
 rra
 scf
 rra
 rra
 and $58
 or b
 ld b,a
 ld a,d
 ld d,b
 add a
 add a
 and $e0
 or e
 ld e,a
(For a full explanation of the logic and motivation behind this code, please see
the original routine
, which takes it apart in detail.)
Copying the Graphics
The actual copy is mostly a simple nested loop, but there’s one nasty trick here. Remember a few sections up where we stored values in the variables
.row_count
and
.stride
? We didn’t declare those in our variable space the way we did for Bresenham’s algorithm. That’s because this code is self-modifying: the variables are written into the constant operands of load instructions. This is another technique that Sjasm makes easier than I made it
when I first discussed the technique
; I can set private equates and define them in terms of the current program counter (represented in Sjasm by
$
):
.col_loop:
 push de ; Save the addr of column top
 ld b,16 ; Load row count
.row_count equ $-1
Actually copying the byte at the start of the loop is simple enough…
.row_loop:
 ld a,(hl) ; Column loop: Load src byte
 inc hl ; Advance src ptr
 ld (de),a ; Store byte at dest
… and we covered how to advance the destination pointer properly last week.
inc d ; Advance dest ptr
ld a,7
and d
jr nz,1F
ld a,e
add 32
ld e,a
jr c,1F
ld a,d
sub 8
ld d,a
1 djnz .row_loop ; Manage rest of column
Once a column is copied, we have to advance the destination pointer. Instead of trying to reverse the work we did above, we just pop our saved value and increment it. We can then also check to see if we’ve wrapped off the right edge here and quit right away if we did.
pop de
 inc de
 ld a,e
 and 31
 ret z
Now we hit the other piece of self-modifying code: we need to update the source pointer by the between-column stride amount.
ld a,0
.stride equ $-1
 add l
 jr nc,1F
 inc h
1 ld l,a
That’s the column loop covered; all we have to do now is loop back and return when done.
dec c
 jr nz,.col_loop
 ret
Overall I’m happy enough with this routine as-is; the one thing I’m worried about before trying to use it in earnest is that it trashes all the registers, including its arguments. If I want to place multiple copies of a sprite, or lay down multiple sprites in the same place or something, this might be meaningfully inconvenient. I guess we’ll see as the project advances.
The Test Program
We won’t be doing much with this program; the general idea will be to have a sprite that takes up the full 16×16 graphics space that we can move around with the keyboard and test to make sure that we leave the screen properly in all directions.
Defining and Baking the Assets
The first thing we have to do is define our graphics and prepare them properly. To animate the sprite, I’ll just be erasing them then redrawing them. This reuses the sprite-shifter from last time and then sets up 192 zero bytes to let us draw as a sprite eraser.
org $7000
 map bss_start
sprite_gfx # 192
blank_gfx # 192

 ;; Make shifted copy of sprite
 ld hl,gfx
 ld ix,sprite_gfx
 call shift_sprite
 ;; Make blank sprite
 ld hl,blank_gfx
 ld b,192
 xor a
1 ld (hl),a
 inc hl
 djnz 1B
At the bottom of the program we define the sprite itself—a simple box with a crosshair through it. We also set the end-of-program label for the initial
MAP
directive.
gfx: defb $ff,$ff,$e0,$d0,$c8,$c4,$c2,$c1,$c1,$c2,$c4,$c8,$d0,$e0,$ff,$ff
 defb $ff,$ff,$07,$0b,$13,$23,$43,$83,$83,$43,$23,$13,$0b,$07,$ff,$ff
bss_start:
Reading the Keyboard
We covered the basics of keyboard reading in
our initial tour
, though we did it both in BASIC and in decimal. Looking up the relevant keys and converting to hexadecimal, we find that Q,A,P, and SPACE are the 1 bit in ports
$FBFE
,
$FDFE
,
$DFFE
, and
$7FFE
respectively, while O is the 2 bit in port
$DFFE
. We also need to remember that the
IN A,(C)
and
OUT (C),A
take a full 16-bit port in
BC
.
We’ll set this up to return DY in H, DX in L, and zero-flag set if Space is pressed. The code itself is straightforward, and very similar to what we saw when reading joysticks.
read_dir:
 ld hl,0
 ld bc,$fbfe ; Check Q
 in a,(c)
 rra
 jr c,1F
 dec h
1 ld b,$fd ; Check A
 in a,(c)
 rra
 jr c,1F
 inc h
1 ld b,$df ; Check P
 in a,(c)
 rra
 jr c,1F
 inc l
1 rra ; Check O
 jr c,1F
 dec l
1 ld b,$7f ; Check SPACE
 in a,(c)
 and 1 ; Set Z if SPACE pressed
 ret
The Main Loop
The main loop mostly just glues everything together. We’ll keep the sprite’s position in
DE
; we can then use
HL
to hold sprite sources and keyboard information as needed. We’ll start each iteration of the main loop by waiting for VBLANK, erasing the sprite at its current position, reading the keyboard, and quitting if the SPACE key is pressed.
;; Initial sprite position
 ld de,$583c

 ;; Main loop
mainlp: halt
 push de
 ld hl,blank_gfx
 call draw_sprite
 call read_dir
 pop de
 jr z,.end
At this point we have our delta-Y in
H
and delta-X in
L
. We’ll need to update the sprite’s location with these and boundary-check them. We handle the Y coordinate first. In order to track the horizontal speed, we double our vertical speed so that diagonal motion stays 45 degrees:
ld a,d
 add h
 add h
 cp -16
 jr nz,1F
 ld a,-14
1 cp 192
 jr nz,1F
 ld a,190
1 ld d,a
The X coordinates are already doubled so we only apply the delta once.
ld a,e
 add l
 cp -8
 jr nz,1F
 ld a,-7
1 cp 128
 jr nz,1F
 ld a,127
1 ld e,a
Then we redraw the sprite and wait for the next frame once again.
push de
 ld hl,sprite_gfx
 call draw_sprite
 pop de
 jr mainlp
.end: ret
Starting the Shooting Gallery
This gives us a direct path into building the shooting gallery, at least at first. We have four sprites (three targets and the blaster) and move and draw them using the same routines we’ve just laid out. It’s a good start, but we do hit a problem pretty quickly: the targets occasionally disappear.
The problem here is that I’m clearing the targets then redrawing them, and the timing of this is consistent enough that there are “blind spots” in the display where objects have been erased but have not yet been properly redrawn. This isn’t really a surprise; the 3.5MHz Z80 in the Spectrum may be clocked much faster than a C64’s 1MHz 6502, but it’s hitting memory much more slowly and there’s no way we’re going to get all our bitmap work before VBLANK is done. This is a bit grim. If we’re
already
pushing the system too hard here, there’s no way we’ll be able to fill the screen with laser blasts to go along with it!
If we can’t get a perfect update, then the best we can do is minimize the damage. We need to be more judicious about how we update the screen, so that if and when the raster scan catches us unprepared, the worst the user sees is some minor tearing or clipping. We have an advantage here, as it happens: we aren’t actually blending our sprites into the screen. Instead, we’re just copying out 24×16 blocks of pixels which obliterate everything that was there previously. Not only that, the way we baked the assets means that an aligned sprite wipes out the 8×16 region to its right. That means that the targets ought to clean up after themselves unless they’re moving up and down, and the blaster cleans up after itself unless it’s moving right.
We’ll tackle these issues next week, along with getting shots working.
